2018 / United Kingdom / Graphic

Data visualizations - Global warming

One of the most iconic data visualizations of the last decade is the Show Your Stripes graphic, representing global warming on a planetary level, between 1850 and 2025, an increase of 1.4°.

Visit project website

The climate stripes were created by Professor Ed Hawkins at the University of Reading in 2018 and have been embraced around the world as a clear and vivid representation of how the climate is changing, and a powerful symbol of efforts of the urgency to address this. The graphic represents global warming on a planetary level, between 1850 and 2025, an increase of 1.4°.

This simple graphic has been shared globally in different media, both digital, textiles, and large-format prints. This graphic has a Creative Commons license, encouraging people to distribute it freely.

Criteria

  • SA1 / SocietyElectronic Documents

    All electronic documents comply with the W3C WCAG 2.0 Level A standard, or higher, or comply with the ISO standard for PDF/UA accessibility standard.

  • SA2 / SocietyPrinted Documents and Compliance

    Printed materials are designed using accessible typography, contrast, hierarchy, and readability principles to support users with visual, cognitive, or literacy-related accessibility needs.

  • SA3 / SocietyUniversal Design Principles

    The non-document components of the project adhere to universal design principles.

  • EIRT1 / EnvironmentEnvironmental Impact Reduction

    The project strategy includes at least one action to reduce environmental impact that is supported by a qualified life cycle study (LCS) or quantitative life cycle assessment (LCA).

  • EEM1 / EnvironmentStorage and Transportation

    The project includes shipping and/or warehousing efficiencies to optimize storage and transportation.

  • FFP2 / FinanceAccountability and Transparency

    Adheres to transparent financial management and documentation practices.

  • E1 / EnvironmentEnvironmental Impact Reduction

    The project strategy includes at least one action to reduce environmental impact that is supported by a qualified life cycle study (LCS) or quantitative life cycle assessment (LCA).

  • E8 / EnvironmentEnvironmental Policy

    The design entity and a majority of suppliers have publicly-accessible environmental policies.

  • EM10 / EnvironmentEcosystems Conservation

    To the best of the design entity's knowledge, the project, the design entity, and the client's activities do not, and will not, support the destruction of ecosystems.

  • E19 / EnvironmentQuantified GHG Reporting and Certification

    Project: The project has a publicly-accessible quantified report of GHG reductions and/or energy, material use and waste disposal. Design Entity: The design entity has a publicly-accessible quantified report of GHG reductions and/or energy, material use and waste disposal.

  • E20 / EnvironmentAir Pollution

    Project: The project reduces or avoids air pollution. Design Entity: The design entity reduces or avoids air pollution.

  • E21 / EnvironmentCarbon Offsets

    Project: The project offsets all GHG emissions for travel, production and Web presence. Design Entity: The design entity offsets all GHG emissions for travel, production and Web presence.

  • C7 / CultureCommunity Participation

    The design entity actively supports and participates in the sustainable development of their community.

  • C8 / CulturePractitioners' Education

    The project results in the education of sustainability for design practitioners.

  • C6 / CultureAudience Engagement

    The project engages end users throughout the design process or audiences that will be directly impacted by the project.

  • S11 / SocietyIntellectual Property

    The project clearly defines and respects intellectual property ownership, authorship, permissions, licensing, and usage rights. Where appropriate, the project may also share reusable intellectual property through Creative Commons or another open licensing approach that creates value for society.

Front-of-Package Food Warning Labels

Across Latin America, food warning labels have become one of the clearest examples of communication design used as part of public health policies. In addition to the use of small nutrition tables, or technical nutrition data, these “Excess Sugar,” “Excess Sodium,” “Excess Calories,” or “Excess Saturated Fats” labels are prominently placed on the front of food and beverage packaging.
